questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of worsening myalgia, restlessness, and sweating. Her jaw had been feeling tight for 2 days, and she felt unable to walk properly due to stiffness. She was a keen gardener. She had a history of hypertension, depression, and gastro-oesophageal reflux. She was taking bendroflumethiazide, sertraline, and ranitidine. On examination she was sitting straight up in bed. Her blood pressure was 138/76 mmHg and her heart rate was 102 beats/minute. She was orientated to time, place, and person. Her face was taut with a wide smile and tense masseters. She was sweating profusely. She had dilated but reactive pupils. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Her skin was intact except for a 6 cm healing laceration along her right shin. Neurologic exam: Diffusely increased tone and rigidity in all muscle groups. Occasional twitches visible. Muscle power 5/5; reflexes brisk but equal; gag reflex elicited a bite. Sensation intact.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tetanus Tetanus is the most likely diagnosis due to risk factors (gender and age mean she is unlikely to have completed a vaccination course; gardening injuries are a recognized route of entry) and to the clinical features of excessive muscle spasm and sympathetic activity. Generalized tetanus is commonly a descending pattern after a nonspecific prodrome of fever, malaise, and headache. Patients are usually cognitively intact. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is most commonly associated with drugs affecting dopamine activity, within 1–4 weeks of initiating or changing dose; it is also usually associated with an altered mental status. She has had no history of exposure to rabies, nor are the classic clinical features of rabies present, such as hydrophobia or insomnia. She has no features of cognitive impairment or confusion that would be expected with a herpes encephalitis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q12

questions.stem: A 37-year-old construction worker presented to the emergency department with fever and painful muscle spasms for 1 day. On examination, his temperature is 38.1°C, pulse 122 beats/minute, blood pressure 135/80 mmHg, and he has a small wound on his hand with surrounding erythema and induration that he says he sustained because of puncturing his hand with a nail.
questions.lead_in: What is the first-line antimicrobial of choice to inhibit further toxin production contributing to his illness?
questions.explanation: Metronidazole Treatment with metronidazole, along with tetanus immune globulin, should be administered. Metronidazole is recommended as first-line antimicrobial therapy for tetanus. The other antibiotics listed are recommended as second-line agents.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q36

questions.question: Tetanus.

parts.text: Why and how does it cause paralysis?

parts_raw.text: Why and how does it cause paralysis

questions.model_answer: a) Clostridium tetani (obligate anaerobic, spore-forming gram-positive bacillus); toxin is tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin). b) Tetanospasmin reaches the CNS by entering presynaptic terminals of lower motor neurons and travelling by retrograde axonal transport to cell bodies in the brainstem and spinal cord; there it degrades synaptobrevin, blocking neurotransmitter vesicle release from inhibitory glycinergic interneurons and descending GABAergic neurons. Loss of this inhibition raises the resting firing rate of motor neurons (rigidity) and exaggerates reflex responses to afferent stimuli (spasms); it is a spastic, not flaccid, paralysis. c) (1) Generalized (2) Localized (3) Cephalic (4) Neonatal. d) (1) Passive immunization with human tetanus immune globulin (HTIG) 500 U IM, plus active immunization with tetanus toxoid at a different site. (2) Control of spasms/rigidity with benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, or midazolam infusion) and airway protection. (3) Antimicrobial therapy with metronidazole 500 mg IV q6h for 7-10 days.

questions.question: Tetanus.

parts.text: Name the bacteria and the toxin involved.
Describe mechanism of action for toxin.

parts_raw.text: Name the bacteria and the toxin involved
Describe mechanism of action for toxin

questions.model_answer: a) Clostridium tetani; toxin tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin), encoded on a plasmid present in all toxigenic strains. b) Toxin enters presynaptic terminals of lower motor neurons and travels by retrograde axonal transport to the brainstem and spinal cord; it then diffuses to inhibitory cells (glycinergic interneurons and descending GABAergic neurons) and degrades synaptobrevin, preventing docking/release of inhibitory neurotransmitter. The disinhibited motor neurons produce rigidity and reflex spasms; the autonomic nervous system is similarly disinhibited, producing a hypersympathetic state. c) (1) Generalized (2) Localized (3) Cephalic (4) Neonatal. d) (1) HTIG 500 U IM to neutralize unbound toxin, with active immunization (tetanus toxoid) given at a separate site with a separate syringe. (2) Metronidazole 500 mg IV q6h for 7-10 days (preferred over penicillin, a GABA_A antagonist). (3) Benzodiazepines (GABA_A agonists) as mainstay to control spasms/rigidity, with airway control and management of autonomic dysfunction.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort states toxin acts at the neuromuscular junction; Mandell localizes the action to inhibitory interneurons of the spinal cord/brainstem (blocking glycine/GABA release), not the NMJ.

cohort_answer.text: Bacteria/toxin: Clostridium tetani; Tetanospasmin (Tetanus Toxin). MOA: Tetanus toxin binds to the presynaptic inhibitory interneuron of the neuromuscular junction and prevents GABA release that would send inhibitory impulses to the motorneuron, thus preventing muscle relaxation. Syndromes: Generalized; Local; Cephalic; Neonatal. Treatment: Administer Human Tetanus Immune globulin at the wound site; Provide Tetanus Immunization at a different site; Provide Antibiotics for 7-10 days (Metronidazole IV preferred)

questions.question: A 6-year-old child presents following a cat bite sustained while playing aggressively with a cat. On examination there are 2 puncture wounds on the left arm, with no surrounding erythema or edema.
questions.question_raw: You see a 6 year-old child presenting following a cat bite, who he was playing “aggressively” with. On examination, there are 2 puncture wounds on the left arm, with no surrounding erythema or edema

parts.text: Presuming no antibiotic allergies, what antibiotic should be given for prophylaxis?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has received all of his routine immunizations except for the pre-school boosters?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has not received any immunizations after 4 months of age?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he is HIV positive and has received all of his routine immunizations except for the pre-school boosters?

parts_raw.text: Presuming no antibiotic allergies, what antibiotic should be given for prophylaxis?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has received all of his routine immunizations except for pre-school boosters?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has not received any immunizations after 4 months?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he is HIV positive has received all of his routine immunizations except for pre-school boosters?

questions.model_answer:
a) Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (first choice for preemptive/prophylactic therapy of terrestrial animal bites); a cat puncture wound is an indication for prophylaxis given the high infection risk and Pasteurella multocida carriage.
b) A puncture bite is a tetanus-prone (not clean-minor) wound. He has had 3 or more prior doses (primary series complete, only the pre-school booster missing), so give a single dose of tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (as the due booster); tetanus immune globulin (TIG) is NOT required.
c) Having received vaccines only to 4 months means fewer than 3 doses (2 doses). For a tetanus-prone wound with fewer than 3 (or uncertain) prior doses, give tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine AND TIG, and complete/continue the primary immunization series.
d) HIV positive counts as impaired immunity: an individual with humoral/immune deficiency who has a wound that is not clean and minor should receive BOTH the tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (the due booster) AND TIG, regardless of time since the last dose.
questions.beyond_mandell: Tetanus toxoid/TIG decision rules (dose thresholds, TIG in immunocompromised) are from the Canadian Immunization Guide, not the Mandell text.

questions.question: Patient with trismus, muscle spasms, etc. What is the diagnosis?
questions.question_raw:
Q33 (2011 PM)
Patient with trismus, muscle spasms etc.
questions.model_answer: a) Generalized tetanus (Clostridium tetani infection). It classically begins with risus sardonicus and trismus (lockjaw), with descending rigidity, opisthotonic/decorticate-type spasms triggered by sensory stimuli, a preserved level of consciousness, and severe pain during spasms.

cohort_answer.text: Clostridium tetani. Generalized tetanus often begins with risus sardonicus and trismus ("lockjaw"). Abdominal rigidity may be present. Spasm resembles decorticate posturing with opisthotonic posturing. Patient does not lose consciousness, experiences severe pain during spasms, often triggered by sensory stimuli. Airway obstruction or diaphragm involvement can compromise respiration. Autonomic dysfunction is leading cause of death.

questions.question: Patient with trismus, muscle spasms, etc. What questions do you ask?
questions.question_raw:
Q33 (2011 PM)
Patient with trismus, muscle spasms etc.

parts_raw.text: B) What questions do you ask?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Portal of entry (wound/injury, including compound fractures, injection drug use). (2) Incubation period (time from inoculation to first symptom) and period of onset (first symptom to first generalized spasm) - shorter intervals indicate worse prognosis. (3) Tetanus immunization history (partial immunity lessens severity).

cohort_answer.text: Portal of entry, incubation period, period of onset, vaccination hx (partial immunity reduces severity)

questions.question: Patient with trismus, muscle spasms, etc. What is the differential diagnosis?
questions.question_raw:
Q33 (2011 PM)
Patient with trismus, muscle spasms etc.
questions.model_answer: a) (1) Strychnine poisoning (glycine antagonism - the only condition that truly mimics tetanus). (2) Dystonic reaction to neuroleptics/central dopamine antagonists (usually with lateral head turning, responds to benztropine/diphenhydramine). (3) Dental infection causing trismus. (4) Other causes of neck stiffness are distinguished by the absence of tetanus's other features.

cohort_answer.text: Drug-induced dystonia; Trismus due to dental infection; Strychnine poisoning (rat poison); Malignant neuroleptic syndrome

questions.question: Patient with trismus, muscle spasms, etc. What microbiologic tests are used for diagnosis?
questions.question_raw:
Q33 (2011 PM)
Patient with trismus, muscle spasms etc.
questions.model_answer: a) None reliably. Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis; laboratory testing can neither confirm nor exclude it. Wound culture for C. tetani is not useful: anaerobic cultures are frequently negative, a positive culture does not show whether the organism carries the toxin-producing plasmid, and a positive culture can occur without disease in immune patients. Toxicologic serum/urine studies (strychnine, dopamine antagonists) are done mainly to exclude mimics.

cohort_answer.text: No specific micro test - clinical dx or EMG (do not attempt to culture from wound - often false +/-). Tetanus is diagnosed clinically; laboratory testing cannot confirm or exclude the condition and is primarily useful for excluding intoxications that mimic tetanus. Attempts to culture C. tetani from wounds are not useful.

questions.question: Patient with trismus, muscle spasms, etc. What non-laboratory test is used for diagnosis?
questions.question_raw:
Q33 (2011 PM)
Patient with trismus, muscle spasms etc.
questions.model_answer: a) Electromyography (EMG) is occasionally useful in questionable cases, particularly when no portal of entry is apparent. Otherwise the diagnosis rests on clinical observation.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell names EMG as the adjunctive non-lab test but does not describe the 'spatula test' the cohort cites; the spatula (touching the posterior pharyngeal wall to provoke masseter contraction) is reported elsewhere (Apte & Karnad).

cohort_answer.text: Spatula test (spec 100%, sens 94%) - touch back of pharyngeal wall, reflex contraction of masseters = positive test, gag reflex is negative. EMG.

questions.question: Patient with trismus, muscle spasms, etc. Describe your approach to treatment across early management, intermediate stage, and convalescence.
questions.question_raw:
Q33 (2011 PM)
Patient with trismus, muscle spasms etc.

parts.text: Approach to treatment (early management, intermediate stage, convalescent).

parts_raw.text: F) Approach to treatment (early management, intermediate stage, convalescent)

questions.model_answer: a) Early (first hour / first 24 h): secure airway and ventilation (orotracheal intubation under sedation and neuromuscular blockade, early tracheostomy if spasms compromise the airway); give a benzodiazepine to control spasms; neutralize toxin with HTIG 500 U IM; give adsorbed tetanus toxoid at a different site; start metronidazole 500 mg IV q6h for 7-10 days; debride wounds as needed; begin nutritional support. Intermediate (next 2-3 weeks): manage autonomic/sympathetic hyperactivity (labetalol or morphine infusion; consider magnesium sulfate; avoid diuretics), treat hypotension/bradycardia, prophylactic heparin, pressure-injury prevention, maintain then taper benzodiazepines over 14-21 days, begin rehabilitation planning. Convalescent (2-6 weeks): physical therapy once spasms resolve, supportive psychotherapy, and complete active immunization (repeat toxoid before discharge, third dose 4 weeks later).

cohort_answer.text: ACUTE: Airway management; muscle relaxation (benzos, sedation with propofol); neutralize toxin (human tetanus immunoglobulin IM with part of dose infiltrating wound); active immunization at 0, 4-6 weeks, 6-12 months and q10 years; stop toxin production (surgical debridement); abx (metronidazole or penicillin x 7-10 days); supportive measures; manage autonomic instability. INTERMEDIATE: complete vaccine series and continue q10 years. CONVALESCENCE: manage complications (fracture of spinal bones, rhabdo, PNA, PE, cerebral palsy in neonates)

questions.question: Tetanus. Name the toxin.
questions.model_answer: a) Tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin), encoded on a plasmid present in all toxigenic strains. (C. tetani also produces tetanolysin, which is of uncertain importance in pathogenesis.)

cohort_answer.text: Tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin). Two toxins, tetanospasmin and tetanolysin, are produced; tetanospasmin is encoded on a plasmid present in all toxigenic strains; tetanolysin is of uncertain importance.

questions.question: Tetanus. Describe the mechanism of action.
questions.model_answer: a) Tetanospasmin enters the CNS via presynaptic terminals of lower motor neurons and is carried by retrograde axonal transport to neuronal cell bodies in the brainstem and spinal cord. It then diffuses to inhibitory cells (local glycinergic interneurons and descending GABAergic neurons) and degrades synaptobrevin, a protein needed for docking of neurotransmitter vesicles, thereby blocking release of inhibitory transmitter. Loss of inhibition raises motor-neuron resting firing (rigidity) and exaggerates reflex responses (spasms); disinhibition of the autonomic system produces a hypersympathetic state. Toxin binding is essentially irreversible.

cohort_answer.text: Toxin enters CNS through presynaptic terminals of LMNs then to spinal cord and brainstem via retrograde axonal transport. Enters interneurons and blocks neurotransmission, net inactivation of inhibitory neurotransmission = loss of inhibition = increased muscle tone, painful spasms, widespread autonomic instability, muscle rigidity

questions.question: Tetanus. List 4 critical therapeutic interventions.
questions.model_answer: a) (1) Airway/ventilation control with spasm management using benzodiazepines (early tracheostomy if needed). (2) Passive immunization with HTIG 500 U IM to neutralize unbound toxin, plus active immunization with tetanus toxoid at a separate site. (3) Antimicrobial therapy with metronidazole 500 mg IV q6h for 7-10 days (plus wound debridement as needed). (4) Management of autonomic dysfunction (e.g., labetalol or morphine infusion, consider magnesium sulfate) with supportive intensive care and nutrition.

cohort_answer.text: ACUTE: Airway management; muscle relaxation; neutralize toxin (human tetanus immunoglobulin); active immunization; stop toxin production (surgical debridement); abx (metronidazole or penicillin x 7-10 days); supportive measures; manage autonomic instability. INTERMEDIATE: complete vaccine series. CONVALESCENCE: manage complications
